claim: Displacement loops (D-loops) are signature intermediates formed during homologous recombination.
source: Displacement loops (D-loops) are signature intermediates formed during homologous recombination.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about D-loops in the field of homologous recombination.

claim: Numerous factors regulate D-loop formation and disruption, thereby influencing crucial aspects of DNA repair, including donor choice and the possibility of crossover outcome.
source: Numerous factors regulate D-loop formation and disruption, thereby influencing crucial aspects of DNA repair, including donor choice and the possibility of crossover outcome.
evidence: This statement draws from established understanding in the field of DNA repair and homologous recombination.

evidence: This claim is supported by the discussion of limitations of current methods in the Introduction section.

claim: A novel in vitro assay was developed to characterize the length and position of individual D-loops with near base-pair resolution and deep coverage.

evidence: This is a primary finding of the manuscript describing the development of the D-loop Mapping Assay.

claim: The D-loop Mapping Assay is widely applicable with different substrates and donor types.

claim: Homologous recombination (HR) is a universal DNA repair pathway that is vital to genome maintenance and the repair of double-stranded DNA breaks, stalled or collapsed forks and inter-strand crosslinks.

evidence: This statement is supported by citations to established literature in the field.

claim: Repair by HR begins by resection of the broken DNA molecule leaving a single-stranded DNA (ssDNA) with a free 3′-OH end.
source: Repair by HR begins by resection of the broken DNA molecule leaving a single-stranded DNA (ssDNA) with a free 3′-OH end.

claim: The Rad51 protein forms a filament on the ssDNA and carries out DNA strand invasion into a homologous duplex donor.
source: The Rad51 protein forms a filament on the ssDNA and carries out DNA strand invasion into a homologous duplex donor.

source: Nicked plasmids would have unrestricted topology, allowing the formation of D-loops that span the entire region of homology.
evidence: This is an inference based on knowledge of DNA topology.

claim: Most of the footprints had the D-loop length expected from the topological limit, suggesting that branch migration, if at all, was minimal on supercoiled donors.
source: Since most of the footprints had the D-loop length expected from the topological limit, it seems that branch migration, if at all, was minimal on supercoiled donors.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data.

claim: No significant changes in D-loop length or position occur during the bisulfite treatment.
source: This suggests that no significant changes in D-loop length or position occur during the bisulfite treatment.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data showing minimal branch migration.

claim: The lack of footprints outside the region of homology, their absence on the bottom-strand, their dependence on the formation of a D-loop, and their uniform length restricted by the supercoiling density of the donor provide high confidence that the footprints represent D-loops.
source: In summary, the lack of footprints outside the region of homology, their absence on the bottom-strand, their dependence on the formation of a D-loop, and their uniform length restricted by the supercoiling density of the donor provide high confidence that the footprints represent D-loops.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on multiple lines of experimental evidence.

claim: A total of ~800–3,700 (10–18%) D-loops were observed among ~4,000–40,000 top-strand reads for D-loops formed on a linear donor.
source: A total of ~800–3,700 (10–18%) D-loops were observed among ~4,000–40,000 top-strand reads (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is experimental data from the study shown in Figure 4B.

claim: While the bottom-strand comprised ~13,000–100,000 reads, it had <0.1% of reads with a footprint.
source: Again, while the bottom-strand comprised ~13,000–100,000 reads, it had <0.1% of reads with a footprint.
evidence: This is experimental data from the study.

claim: Even with a linear, topologically unrestricted donor, the D-loops were mapped with high strand-specificity (>100 fold).
source: Thus, even with a linear, topologically unrestricted donor, the D-loops were mapped with high strand-specificity (>100 fold).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data comparing top and bottom strand footprints.

claim: Relative D-loop levels quantified from DMA correlated with the D-loop levels from the gel-based assay.
source: Relative D-loop levels quantified from DMA correlated with the D-loop levels from the gel-based assay (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This is a comparison of experimental data from DMA and gel-based assays shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: The D-loop footprints were essentially all found within the window of homology for each substrate type.
source: Moreover, the D-loop footprints were essentially all found within the window of homology for each substrate type, as evident from individual footprint maps (Figure 4C, Figure 4—figure supplement 2A–C), attesting to the homology-specificity of the footprints.
evidence: This is experimental data from the study shown in Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 2A–C.

claim: The distribution of the D-loop position with a linear donor revealed an enrichment at the 3′-end of homology, similar to the D-loops formed using a supercoiled donor.
source: Next, the distribution of the D-loop position with a linear donor revealed an enrichment at the 3′-end of homology (Figure 4D, Figure 4—figure supplement 2D,E), similar to the D-loops formed using a supercoiled donor.
evidence: This is experimental data from the study shown in Figure 4D and Figure 4—figure supplement 2D,E.

claim: The presence of a non-homologous 3′-flap in ds98-915-78ss sample did not significantly alter the distribution of the D-loop position compared to the ds98-915 sample.
source: Moreover, the presence of a non-homologous 3′-flap in ds98-915-78ss sample did not significantly alter the distribution of the D-loop position (Figure 4D) compared to the ds98-915 sample.
evidence: This is experimental data from the study shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The distribution of D-loops was unaltered by changes in the homology sequence between the ds98-931 and ds98-915 substrates.
source: The distribution of D-loops was also unaltered by changes in the homology sequence between the ds98-931 and ds98-915 substrates (Figure 4D, Figure 4—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: This is experimental data from the study shown in Figure 4D and Figure 4—figure supplement 2D.

claim: Differences in cytosine distribution across the homology do not significantly alter D-loop distribution, as long as the % CG is not very low.
source: This suggests that differences in cytosine distribution across the homology do not significantly alter D-loop distribution, as long as the % CG is not very low.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data comparing different substrates.

claim: There was no preferred D-loop length with a linear donor; instead, a broad range of D-loop lengths was observed, independent of the substrate type.
source: Interestingly, there was no preferred D-loop length. Instead, a broad range of D-loop lengths was observed, independent of the substrate type (Figure 4E,F).
evidence: This is experimental data from the study shown in Figure 4E,F.

claim: The lengths of the D-loops ranged from ~100 nt to a maximum spanning the entire length of homology.
source: The lengths of the D-loops ranged from ~100 nt to a maximum spanning the entire length of homology.
evidence: This is experimental data from the study.

claim: D-loops as long as 900 nt were seen with the long substrates (ds98-915, ds98-931, and ds98-915-78ss) at a frequency of ~5% of the total D-loops.
source: D-loops as long as 900 nt were seen with the long substrates (ds98-915, ds98-931, and ds98-915-78ss) at a frequency of ~5% of the total D-loops (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is experimental data from the study shown in Figure 4E.

claim: The minimum D-loop size of 100 nt is limited by the peak threshold (of t40w50) used to define a D-loop footprint.
source: The minimum D-loop size of 100 nt is limited by the peak threshold (of t40w50) used to define a D-loop footprint.
evidence: This is an explanation of a methodological limitation.

claim: An average D-loop length of ~390 nt was noted with the 900 nt homology series substrates.
source: An average D-loop length of ~390 nt was noted with the 900 nt homology series substrates.
evidence: This is experimental data from the study.

claim: There was a slight, yet significant difference in the D-loop lengths between the ds98-915 and ds98-931, with a difference in mean of 60 nt.
source: There was a slight, yet significant difference in the D-loop lengths between the ds98-915 and ds98-931, with a difference in mean of 60 nt.
evidence: This is experimental data from the study.

claim: There was no statistical difference in D-loop lengths between the ds98-915 and ds98-915-78ss substrates, suggesting that the 78 nt 3′-flap does not alter D-loop lengths.
source: However, there was no statistical difference in D-loop lengths between the ds98-915 and ds98-915-78ss substrates, suggesting that the 78 nt 3′-flap does not alter D-loop lengths.
evidence: This is experimental data from the study.

claim: The average D-loop length decreased from ~390 nt to ~320 nt, when the homology length was reduced to 607 nt using the ds98-607 substrate.
source: As expected, the average D-loop length decreased from ~390 nt to ~320 nt, when the homology length was reduced to 607 nt using the ds98-607 substrate (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is experimental data from the study shown in Figure 4F.

claim: The maximum D-loop length for the ds98-607 substrate was 600 nt, restricted only by the homology length.
source: The maximum D-loop length for the ds98-607 substrate was 600 nt, restricted only by the homology length.
evidence: This is experimental data from the study.

claim: About 6% of the D-loops were longer than 500 nt, traversing across the region of homology for the ds98-607 substrate.
source: About 6% of the D-loops were longer than 500 nt, traversing across the region of homology.
evidence: This is experimental data from the study.

claim: The D-loops formed with the ds98-197-78ss substrate had an average length of 176 nt, and ~73% spanned the entire region of homology.
source: Similarly, the D-loops formed with the ds98-197-78ss substrate had an average length of 176 nt, and ~73% spanned the entire region of homology.
evidence: This is experimental data from the study.

claim: Homology length defines the maximum observable D-loop length, and in turn, influences the average D-loop length.
source: In summary, our results demonstrate that homology length defines the maximum observable D-loop length, and in turn, influences the average D-loop length.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data showing the relationship between homology length and D-loop length.

claim: D-loops formed on a linear donor are relatively less stable than those on a supercoiled donor.
source: Note that since the D-loops formed on a linear donor are relatively less stable than those on a supercoiled donor (Wright and Heyer, 2014), it is possible that the footprints may reflect all changes in D-loop length and position that occurred over the course of the bisulfite treatment.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Formation of multi-invasions, where a single substrate forms D-loops simultaneously in multiple donor molecules, was shown both in vitro and in vivo.
source: Formation of multi-invasions, where a single substrate forms D-loops simultaneously in multiple donor molecules, was shown both in vitro and in vivo (Wright and Heyer, 2014; Piazza et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: Multi-invasions cannot be detected by this assay, since each donor molecule is separately analyzed.
source: However, multi-invasions cannot be detected by this assay, since each donor molecule is separately analyzed.
evidence: This describes a limitation of the assay.

claim: In some cases (~2–5%), multiple D-loop footprints are seen within a single read, representing a single donor.
source: Instead, in some cases (~2–5%), multiple D-loop footprints are seen within a single read (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A–C), representing a single donor.
evidence: This is experimental data from the study shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A–C.

claim: Multiple D-loop footprints within a single read may be due to multiple invasions of one or more substrates into a single donor at two different sites.
source: This may be due to multiple invasions of one or more substrates into a single donor at two different sites (Figure 4—figure supplement 2F).
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed multiple footprints.

claim: The D-loop footprints were specifically seen within the homologous region for D-loops formed using human proteins with both donor types.
source: With both donor types, the D-loop footprints were again specifically seen within the homologous region (Figure 4—figure supplement 3B,D) and on the top strand (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is experimental data from the study shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3B,D and Supplementary file 1.

claim: The distribution of D-loops formed by human proteins was similar to the D-loops produced by the yeast proteins.
source: The distribution of D-loops was similar to the D-loops produced by the yeast proteins.
evidence: This is a comparison of experimental data from human and yeast proteins.

claim: An enrichment of D-loops was seen at the 3′-end of homology with human proteins, irrespective of the donor type.
source: An enrichment of D-loops was seen at the 3′-end of homology, irrespective of the donor type (Figure 4—figure supplement 3E).
evidence: This is experimental data from the study shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3E.

claim: Average D-loop length seen with a supercoiled donor using human proteins was 252 ± 78 nt as expected, while with a linear donor, the average length was 320 ± 140 nt.
source: Average D-loop length seen with a supercoiled donor was 252 ± 78 nt as expected, while with a linear donor, the average length was 320 ± 140 nt (Figure 4—figure supplement 3F).
evidence: This is experimental data from the study shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3F.

claim: The average D-loop length from a linear donor with human proteins was slightly lower than the 410 nt seen with yeast proteins.
source: The average D-loop length from a linear donor was slightly lower than the 410 nt seen with yeast proteins.
evidence: This is a comparison of experimental data from human and yeast proteins.

claim: Only 21% of the D-loops were longer than 400 nt with human recombinant proteins compared to >40% seen with yeast recombinants.
source: Conformingly, only 21% of the D-loops were longer than 400 nt with human recombinant proteins compared to >40% seen with yeast recombinants.
evidence: This is a comparison of experimental data from human and yeast proteins.

claim: Compared to the yeast proteins, human proteins seemed to be less efficient under the conditions used in forming longer D-loops.
source: Thus, compared to the yeast proteins, human proteins seemed to be less efficient under the conditions used in forming longer D-loops.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data comparing human and yeast proteins.

claim: The efficiency of D-loop formation with human proteins was much lower, with only 3% using a linear donor.
source: As evident from observation of the D-loops on an agarose gel (Figure 4—figure supplement 3G,H), the efficiency of D-loop formation was also much lower, with only 3% using a linear donor.
evidence: This is experimental data from the study shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3G,H.

claim: The poor D-loop formation efficiency with human proteins could be due to the poor stability of the RAD51 filament.
source: This could be due to the poor stability of the RAD51 filament.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed low efficiency.

claim: The poor D-loop formation efficiency with human proteins may suggest a role for RAD51 accessory factors in stabilizing the RAD51 filament and altering its properties to promote more efficient D-loop formation.
source: It may also suggest a role for RAD51 accessory factors in stabilizing the RAD51 filament and altering its properties to promote more efficient D-loop formation (San Filippo et al., 2008).
evidence: This is a speculative explanation supported by a citation.

claim: The percentage of D-loops observed on a gel correlated well with the frequency of D-loop footprint for human proteins.
source: Concomitantly, the percentage of D-loops observed on a gel correlated well with the frequency of D-loop footprint (Figure 4—figure supplement 3H).
evidence: This is a comparison of experimental data from gel-based and DMA assays shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3H.

claim: The D-loop Mapping Assay can be broadly used to test the effect of recombinant proteins across various species on D-loop properties.
source: Thus, the D-loop Mapping Assay can be broadly used to test the effect of recombinant proteins across various species on D-loop properties.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data showing the assay works with both yeast and human proteins.

claim: Bisulfite conversion is most efficient at 70°C for 30 min.
source: The bisulfite conversion is most efficient at 70°C for 30 min (Yi et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to established literature.

claim: High temperatures (70°C) would be deleterious for D-loop mapping as it would cause D-loop dissolution or increased DNA breathing.
source: Such high temperatures would be deleterious for our purpose as it would cause D-loop dissolution (Wright and Heyer, 2014) or increased DNA breathing.
evidence: This is an inference based on knowledge of D-loop stability and a citation.

claim: A 4 hr incubation at 37°C showed cytosine conversion patches even outside the homologous region and on the bottom-strand, indicating enhanced DNA breathing at 37°C.
source: A 4 hr incubation at 37°C showed cytosine conversion patches even outside the homologous region and on the bottom-strand (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A), indicating enhanced DNA breathing at 37°C (note that the number of reads analyzed was lower as the lower throughput RS-II sequencing platform was used).
evidence: This is experimental data from the study shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Incubation at 37°C is known to enhance D-loop migration and dissolution.
source: Incubation at 37°C is also known to enhance D-loop migration and dissolution (Wright and Heyer, 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to established literature.

claim: Bisulfite treatment at 37°C for 30 min and at RT for 3 hr showed better recovery of D-loops compared to other treatment conditions.
source: Bisulfite treatment at 37°C for 30 min and at RT for 3 hr showed better recovery of D-loops compared to other treatment conditions (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–C), depicting a higher fraction of reads with a D-loop footprint.
evidence: This is experimental data from the study shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–C.

claim: To minimize potential D-loop migration, a 3 hr incubation at RT was chosen as the optimal condition for the bisulfite treatment.
source: To minimize potential D-loop migration, we opted for a 3 hr incubation at RT as the optimal condition for the bisulfite treatment.
evidence: This describes the methodological choice based on experimental optimization.

claim: 58% of the 420 cytosines were converted on average in each individual read of spiked-in ssDNA, and 100% of the 21 reads had cytosine conversion.
source: 58% of the 420 cytosines were converted on average in each individual read, and 100% of the 21 reads had cytosine conversion (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A,B).
evidence: This is experimental data from the study shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2A,B.

claim: The cumulative cytosine conversion efficiency was 58%.
source: The cumulative cytosine conversion efficiency was thus, 58%.
evidence: This is experimental data from the study.

claim: Choosing a 't' value lower than 58% should prevent false elimination of true footprints.
source: This finding implies that choosing a 't' value lower than 58% should prevent false elimination of true footprints.
evidence: This is an inference based on the measured conversion efficiency.

claim: With peak thresholds of t40w50 and t60w20, almost no footprints were observed on the bottom-strand or in the flanking non-homologous regions for a D-loop sample.
source: For a D-loop sample, with peak thresholds of t40w50 and t60w20, almost no footprints were observed on the bottom-strand or in the flanking non-homologous regions (Figure 5A, Figure 5—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is experimental data from the study shown in Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 2C.

claim: With t40w20, 1.4% of bottom-strand reads had non-specific footprints.
source: With t40w20, 1.4% of bottom-strand reads had such non-specific footprints.
evidence: This is experimental data from the study.

claim: Lowering the conversion frequency (t) to 25% significantly increased footprints on the bottom-strand, along with a concomitant increase in the percent of footprints detected on the top strand.
source: Lowering the conversion frequency (t) to 25% significantly increased footprints on the bottom-strand, along with a concomitant increase in the percent of footprints detected on the top strand.
evidence: This is experimental data from the study.

claim: 11.6% and 8.8% of bottom-strand reads had a footprint with t25w20 and t25w50, respectively, compared to ~40% top-strand footprints.
source: 11.6% and 8.8% of bottom-strand reads had a footprint with t25w20 and t25w50, respectively, compared to ~40% top-strand footprints (Figure 5A, Figure 5—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is experimental data from the study shown in Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 2C.

claim: At least a t40 conversion threshold is required to eliminate the majority of footprints arising from spontaneous DNA breathing.
source: We conclude that at least a t40 conversion threshold is required to eliminate the majority of footprints arising from spontaneous DNA breathing.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data testing different thresholds.

claim: The t40w50 peak threshold is the most optimal for detecting D-loop footprints with respect to specificity.
source: Thus, with respect to specificity, the t40w50 peak threshold is the most optimal for detecting D-loop footprints.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data testing different thresholds.

claim: With t60w20, most of the genuine top-strand D-loop footprints were lost, reducing the percentage of D-loops to 8%.
source: While t60w20 also eliminated background footprints, the frequency 't' requirement was higher than the average conversion frequency seen. Hence, most of the genuine top-strand D-loop footprints were lost, reducing the percentage of D-loops to 8% (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is experimental data from the study shown in Figure 5A.

claim: At the t25w20 threshold, a large number of bottom-strand reads showed two footprints within a read.
source: Interestingly, while the t40w50 threshold eliminates the majority of bottom-strand footprints, at the t25w20 threshold, a large number of bottom-strand reads showed two footprints within a read (Figure 5—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is experimental data from the study shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Two short footprints within a single bottom-strand read may have arisen at the two junctions of a D-loop, where the bottom-strand may be single-stranded.
source: These two short footprints within a single read may have arisen at the two junctions of a D-loop, where the bottom-strand may be single-stranded (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed footprints.

claim: RPA may bind at the 3′ junction of a D-loop, indicating that at least 25 nt single-stranded region may be present on the bottom-strand.
source: RPA may bind at the 3′ junction of a D-loop (Sneeden et al., 2013), indicating that at least 25 nt (the binding site size of RPA) single-stranded region may be present on the bottom-strand.
evidence: This is an inference based on knowledge of RPA binding and a citation.

claim: With t25w50, 22% of the footprints were shorter than 250 nt, compared to 5% with a t40w50 threshold.
source: With t25w50, 22% of the footprints were shorter than 250 nt, compared to 5% with a t40w50 threshold.
evidence: This is experimental data from the study.

claim: The average D-loop length with a t25w50 threshold was 357 nt compared to 410 nt with a t40w50 threshold.
source: Consequently, the average D-loop length with a t25w50 threshold was 357 nt compared to 410 nt with a t40w50 threshold (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is experimental data from the study shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Lowering the window size from w50 to w20 further lowered the average D-loop length.
source: Additionally, lowering the window size from w50 to w20 further lowered the average D-loop length.
evidence: This is experimental data from the study.

claim: The average length was 220 nt for t40w20, with 59% of the D-loops being shorter than 200 nt.
source: The average length was 220 nt for t40w20, with 59% of the D-loops being shorter than 200 nt.
evidence: This is experimental data from the study.

claim: Changes in peak threshold did not affect the overall distribution of D-loops within the homology window.
source: Lastly, changes in peak threshold did not affect the overall distribution of D-loops within the homology window (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is experimental data from the study shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Despite the detection of short non-specific footprints at lower thresholds, there was no bias in the position of these non-specific footprints, meaning that there was no overall change in their distribution.
source: Thus, despite the detection of short non-specific footprints at lower thresholds, there was no bias in the position of these non-specific footprints, meaning that there was no overall change in their distribution.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data testing different thresholds.

claim: The method provides information on individual D-loop molecules with almost base-pair precision.
source: The method provides information on individual D-loop molecules with almost base-pair precision.
evidence: This describes a characteristic of the developed method.

claim: The method is high-throughput, sensitive, and readily applicable to various kinds of D-loops.
source: The method is high-throughput, sensitive, and readily applicable to various kinds of D-loops.
evidence: This describes characteristics of the developed method.

claim: The assay can be broadly used to test the effect of various homologous recombination factors on D-loop characteristics.
source: It can be broadly used to test the effect of various homologous recombination factors on D-loop characteristics.
evidence: This describes the potential applications of the developed method.

claim: It is possible to extend the assay to map other DNA intermediates/structures that include some regions of ssDNA.
source: It is also possible to extend the assay to map other DNA intermediates/structures that include some regions of ssDNA.
evidence: This describes the potential applications of the developed method.

claim: Using the D-loop Mapping Assay, it was shown that Rdh54/Tid1 antagonizes Rad54 in D-loop formation and restricts D-loops length.
source: Using the D-loop Mapping Assay we could show that Rdh54/Tid1 antagonizes Rad54 in D-loop formation and restricts D-loops length (Shah et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to work using the developed method.

claim: Without a topological barrier, D-loop length can vary widely, in some cases stretching as long as the homology permits.
source: Using the novel DMA, we have shown that without a topological barrier, D-loop length can vary widely, in some cases stretching as long as the homology permits.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data with linear donors.

claim: Differences in D-loop length may either reflect differential Rad51 filament lengths or variations in the processivity of Rad54 in forming hDNA.
source: These differences in D-loop length may either reflect differential Rad51 filament lengths or variations in the processivity of Rad54 in forming hDNA.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed variation in D-loop lengths.

claim: The D-loops are enriched at the 3′-end of homology, similar to previous observations.
source: Moreover, the D-loops are enriched at the 3′-end of homology, similar to previous observations (Wright and Heyer, 2014).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data and supported by a citation.

claim: The 3′ enrichment confirms the directionality of the Rad51 filament in a 5′-to-3′ direction.
source: This enrichment confirms the directionality of the Rad51 filament in a 5′-to-3′ direction (Qiu et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data and supported by a citation.

claim: The 3′ enrichment may suggest that the branchpoint with the 3′-OH end of ssDNA better activates the motor activity of the Rad54 translocase.
source: The 3′ enrichment may also suggest that the branchpoint with the 3′-OH end of ssDNA better activates the motor activity of the Rad54 translocase.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed enrichment.

claim: The presence or absence of a topological barrier does not alter the distribution of the D-loop position across the region of homology.
source: Furthermore, the presence or absence of a topological barrier also does not alter the distribution of the D-loop position across the region of homology.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data comparing supercoiled and linear donors.

claim: The D-loops are enriched at the 3′-end, irrespective of topological barriers or D-loop size.
source: The D-loops are enriched at the 3′-end, irrespective of topological barriers or D-loop size.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data.

claim: The presence of a 78 nt non-homologous 3′-flap has no significant effect on the distribution of D-loop length or position.
source: Lastly, the presence of a 78 nt non-homologous 3′-flap has no significant effect on the distribution of D-loop length or position.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data comparing substrates with and without a 3′-flap.
